opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difficulty is that the line between "safety" and "capabilities" is really blurry, and it gets blurrier the closer you look.

Take something like RLHF. It started as an alignment technique, a way to get models to do what we actually want instead of just predicting text. But it's also a big part of what made these models commercially useful. So is that safety compute or capabilities compute? Same with interpretability: if you understand what's going on inside a model, that helps you catch deception, but it also might help you train better models. And on the other side, a lot of what companies call capabilities work, like making models more reliable or better at following instructions, plausibly has safety benefits too.

So if you write a law that says "spend 50% on safety," you've basically created a huge incentive to relabel things. Every company will discover that a remarkable fraction of what it was already doing counts as safety. A regulator would need deep technical expertise and a lot of access to adjudicate that, and even then the categories are contested among researchers in good faith, not just by people trying to game it.

There's a second issue, which is that inputs aren't really what we care about. What we care about is whether the systems being deployed are actually safe, whether we can tell if they're trying to deceive us, whether they could cause catastrophic harm. You could spend half your compute on safety and still do it badly, or spend much less and do it well. A compute ratio is a proxy, and proxies get Goodharted.

That's part of why I've been more drawn to approaches built around outcomes and evidence: if you want to train or deploy a model past some capability threshold, you need to show certain things about it. Things like dangerous capability evaluations, or affirmative safety cases, where the burden is on the developer to demonstrate that the risks are under control. That's harder to fake by relabeling budget lines.

I don't want to be totally dismissive, though. I do think the intuition behind the proposal is right: the ratio of effort going into making these systems more powerful versus making sure we understand and control them is badly lopsided right now. I just think the way to fix that is to make safety a binding constraint on progress, so companies have to invest in it to move forward, rather than mandating a spending number and hoping it translates into something real.

r001.rationale: The response says the boundary between safety and capabilities is blurry and explains that companies could relabel existing work as safety, making the category hard to define.

r002.rationale: It says regulators would need deep technical expertise and substantial access, but does not say that expertise exceeds what currently available regulators have.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest difficulty is just that the line between "safety" and "capabilities" is really blurry, and a lot of the most important safety work doesn't look like a separable bucket of compute you can point to.

Take something like RLHF or whatever the current alignment-training technique is. Is that safety or capabilities? It makes the model more useful, so people deploy it more, but it's also the main lever we have for making the model behave the way we want. Interpretability research is maybe the cleanest case of "pure safety," but even there, if you really understood what was going on inside these models, that would almost certainly feed back into making them more capable. And on the flip side, a lot of capabilities work, like just making the model smarter and less confused, reduces certain kinds of risk from the model doing dumb, unintended things. So if you write a law that says fifty percent goes to safety, you immediately get a huge fight over accounting, and companies have strong incentives to classify things generously.

The second problem is that compute isn't really the bottleneck for most safety research right now. A lot of the alignment work people care about is researcher-hours and good ideas, not enormous training runs. If you forced a lab to burn half its compute on something labeled safety, I think you'd mostly get a lot of wasteful experiments run to hit a quota, rather than better safety outcomes. It's a bit like mandating that a hospital spend half its budget on the pharmacy. That's not obviously what gets you better patient outcomes.

And then there's the enforcement and competition piece. If one jurisdiction does this and others don't, you've basically handicapped the compliant labs without changing the frontier, which could be actively bad if you think the more safety-focused labs being at the frontier matters.

So I'm pretty sympathetic to the intuition behind it, which is that right now the ratio of effort going into "make it more powerful" versus "make sure we understand and control it" seems way off. I just think the lever you want is more like requiring that labs meet certain demonstrable standards before deploying or scaling, with real evaluations and some external oversight, rather than mandating an input ratio. Regulate the outcome you care about, not a proxy that's easy to game and hard to define.

r001.rationale: The response says the line between safety and capabilities is blurry and that a law would spark disputes over how to classify and account for work.

r002.rationale: The response discusses classification disputes, incentives, and enforcement, but does not say regulators lack the technical expertise to enforce the requirement.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difficulty is defining what counts as safety research, because safety and capabilities aren’t cleanly separable. If you’re training a model to follow instructions more reliably, that could make it safer, but it also makes it a more useful product. So does that compute count toward your safety budget?

You could end up with companies relabeling work they would have done anyway, without necessarily being dishonest about it. A lot of work really does serve both purposes. And then you need a regulator to make fairly subtle technical judgments about which projects count and how much credit they get.

I’d be more interested in requiring evidence that a system meets particular safety standards before it’s deployed. Spending half your compute on safety is an input; it doesn’t by itself tell you whether you’ve addressed the risks. You could spend that much and still have a dangerous system, or find a valuable safety intervention that doesn’t require much compute at all.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly identifies defining what counts as safety research as a difficulty with the half-compute requirement.

r002.rationale: It says regulators would need to make subtle technical judgments, but does not say this expertise exceeds what currently available regulators have.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difficulty is that safety and capabilities aren’t cleanly separable categories. If you spend compute training a model to follow instructions more reliably, that can make it safer, but it also makes it a more useful product. And if you train a more capable model, that model might help you do safety research. So it’s hard to say which bucket a particular expenditure belongs in.

If you make that distinction legally consequential, companies have a strong incentive to describe whatever they were going to do anyway as safety work. You could end up with a lot of spending that technically satisfies the requirement without doing much to reduce the risks we care about.

I’d be more interested in requirements that ask companies to demonstrate that they can manage particular risks, and let them figure out how to allocate resources to meet those requirements. That’s also difficult, because we need good ways to evaluate those risks. But I don’t think specifying a fraction of compute gets us around that underlying problem.

r001.rationale: The response says safety and capabilities are not cleanly separable, making it hard to decide which expenditures count as safety work under the 50% requirement.

r002.rationale: It notes that classifying spending and evaluating risks are difficult, but does not say enforcement would require technical expertise beyond what regulators currently have.
